column1: # Every claim this project makes that something can check, and the check.
# ONE ROW PER CLAIM. Tab-separated: id, tags, speed, claim, command.
# WHY IT IS A FILE AND NOT A SCRIPT
# A fix for one fault quietly removed the repair from a mount rung and broke
# dirty-NTFS repair -- a thing proven weeks earlier and still written down as
# proven. Nothing caught it, because what recorded the claim was prose, and
# prose has to be re-read and believed by whoever comes next. After a
# compaction, or in a new session, there is nobody left who remembers to.
# A row here is different: verify.sh runs it, and a claim that no longer holds
# says so without anyone having to remember it existed.
# ADDING ONE. When a bug is fixed, or a behaviour is proven, add a row. If the
# claim has no check yet, still add the row and leave the command empty -- an
# unchecked claim then appears in the list as unchecked, which is the honest
# state and is visible rather than assumed.
# The `hardware` tag needs a drive plugged in and LUKOTTA_TEST_DEVICE naming
# it. That row cannot pass on fixtures and must never be made to: a disk
# image cannot show the durability fault at all, because imago's writes to a
# file land in the kernel's page cache and survive the process dying. It is
# the one claim here that only real hardware can answer.
# TAGS are free-form and comma-separated. "goal" is the owner's ten items;
# anything else -- release, privacy, engine, ui -- is its own set, and
# `TAG=release ./scripts/verify.sh` runs just that one. The point is that this
# outlives any particular list of goals: a task that proves something adds its
# row and the row is checked from then on.
# SPEED is fast, slow or long. Anything but fast needs FULL=1, so the fast
# gate stays quick enough to run on every change. long is for checks that
# genuinely run past half an hour -- launching several apps, each booting a
# machine -- so a real hang is still told apart from a long job.
